 Home India Petrol export duty scrapped, diesel and ATF levies hiked: What it means for consumers in India Petrol export duty scrapped, diesel and ATF levies hiked: What it means for consumers in India
 Open Bureau Last Updated: October 31, 2026, 16:08 IST Summarise Share Share The Centre has removed the special duty on petrol exports but raised levies on diesel and aviation fuel. Here is why the changes matter for domestic fuel supplies, pump prices and airfares. Under the revised rates, the SAED on petrol exports has been cut to zero from Rs 2.5 per litre   Credits: ANI A change in fuel taxes does not always mean a change at the petrol pump. The Centre’s latest revision of export duties on petroleum products, effective October 31, has removed the special additional excise duty (SAED) on petrol exports while increasing the levy on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF). For consumers, the important distinction is that these are duties on fuel sent abroad, not new taxes on petrol or diesel sold in India.

But will motorists pay more, or could airline passengers feel the impact? The answer depends on how refiners and the wider energy market respond.

 Under the revised rates, the SAED on petrol exports has been cut to zero from Rs 2.5 per litre. The duty on high-speed diesel exports has gone up from Rs 8.5 to Rs 11.5 per litre, while the levy on ATF exports has increased from Rs 10.5 to Rs 11 per litre.

Seven Things to Know About the Kirana Push QUICK TAKE | Delhi-NCR’s 50% Work-From-Home Order: Seven Things to Know Amit Shah Pays Tribute to Sardar Patel: ‘In Just 1,218 Days, He Forged a United India’ PM Modi Congratulates ISRO Scientists on Successful NVS-03 Launch Helicopter With 6 on Board Crashes Near Joshimath in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli The revised rates took effect on October 31. The changes follow the previous revision on October 16, when the government had set the respective export levies at Rs 2.5, Rs 8.5 and Rs 10.5 per litre.
 The latest decision is not a uniform increase or reduction in fuel taxes. Instead, it changes the cost of exporting each product differently, reflecting the government’s fortnightly review of international crude oil and refined fuel prices.
 Will petrol and diesel prices rise at Indian fuel stations? 
 For motorists, the immediate answer is no direct increase from this notification. The revised SAED rates apply to exports. They do not impose an additional tax on petrol or diesel purchased for domestic consumption.
 That distinction matters because retail fuel prices are influenced by several factors, including international crude oil prices, refining and transportation costs, dealer commissions, central excise duty and state-level VAT. A change in export duty does not automatically translate into a change in the price displayed at fuel stations.
 The government had also clarified during its March 2026 measures that export levies were separate from duties on domestic fuel sales. Therefore, consumers should not interpret the latest revision as an announcement of an immediate petrol or diesel price hike.
 Why did the Centre introduce export duties in the first place? 
 The export levy framework was introduced on March 27, 2026, as the West Asia crisis heightened concerns about energy supplies and pushed up international prices. The government said higher overseas prices could encourage Indian refiners to export more fuel rather than sell it in the domestic market.
 The objective was to discourage excessive exports and prioritise domestic availability. The petrol export levy was introduced subsequently, as rates were adjusted in response to changing market conditions.
 Since then, the government has reviewed the duties every fortnight, using average international prices of crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF as reference points. The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell’s historical rate table records the repeated revisions.
 Could higher diesel and ATF duties affect transport costs and airfares? 
 The higher export levy could make overseas sales of Indian diesel and ATF less attractive, potentially encouraging refiners to prioritise domestic buyers. That may help support local availability, although the actual impact will depend on production, demand and international prices.
 For consumers, diesel matters well beyond private vehicles. It powers a large part of road freight and is used across sectors such as agriculture and industry. Any sustained change in diesel availability or prices can influence the cost of moving goods and, eventually, the prices consumers pay.
 ATF is a major operating expense for airlines. However, the revised duty applies to exported aviation fuel, not directly to fuel purchased by domestic airlines. It does not, by itself, mean airfares will rise. Ticket prices also depend on domestic ATF rates, crude prices, currency movements and airline operating costs.
 For now, the clearest takeaway is that the October 31 decision changes the economics of exporting fuel, not the tax charged to consumers at the pump. Its wider impact will depend on whether the new rates help strengthen domestic supplies and how global energy prices move in the weeks ahead.
